rejected.title: Naming techniques in analysis
card: Metalanguage is the set of terms we use to talk about language. Simile, personification, first person and alliteration are all metalanguage.
Naming a technique precisely is better than a vague label. Saying "the writer uses a simile" tells a reader more than "the writer uses description".
Naming is only the first step. Analysis also explains the effect: what the technique makes a reader think, feel or picture.
A clear sentence of analysis does both. Example: The simile in "quiet as a held breath" makes the room feel tense.
rejected.remember: Name the technique precisely, then explain its effect on the reader.

a.q: Which sentence of analysis uses metalanguage and explains an effect?
opts: The personification of the wind makes the night menacing
The writer uses nice words to make the night feel scary
The wind howls in the night and the writer describes it well
The writer uses personification, a technique used in English
a.why: It names the technique (personification) and says what it does to the reader. The second option gives an effect but does not name a technique. The last option names one but gives no effect.
a.clue: Look for a precise term and a reason it matters to the reader.

b.q: Mia writes: "The writer uses a metaphor." What should she add to turn this into analysis?
opts: What the metaphor makes the reader feel or picture
A second technique name, such as simile, as well
A retelling of the part of the story it appears in
A comment that the metaphor is a good choice
b.why: Analysis needs the effect of the technique on the reader. Adding a second name or retelling the story does not explain an effect. Saying it is good is vague and gives no reason.
b.clue: Naming is the first step. What is the second?
